newsitem.title: UK: Major defends wait-and-see stance on EU currency.
newsitem.headline: Major defends wait-and-see stance on EU currency.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major, fighting to prevent damaging rows over the European Union at next week's pre-election Conservative Party conference, is strongly defending his "wait-and-see" stance towards a single currency.
"The right course must be to make our choice only when the issues are clear," the British prime minister wrote in an article appearing in the Times newspaper on Saturday.
The so-called Eurosceptic wing of Major's party has been making increasingly strident calls for him to rule out Britain joining a single EU currency at least for the next parliament.

Party managers fear that such calls could bring an embarrassing display of disunity at the conference, which is designed to be a launchpad for the Conservatives' campaign to be reelected at an general election due by next May.
The Conservatives currently trail the opposition Labour Party by more than 20 points in the opinion polls.

Major, whose article appeared as he travelled to Dublin for a one-day EU summit, said the balance of advantage for Britain's business community or for its huge financial services industry between going into a single currency and staying out was still unclear.
But it was vital that Britain should remain in the negotiations on how the currency would operate.
He said if the single currency failed, it would be a "disaster" for Britain whether it was a member or not, given the intertwined nature of the major European economies.
"If they destabilise their economies and the single (EU) market...the British economy will suffer as well," Major said.
"To rush into a premature decision to detach ourselves from the debate about Europe's future would mean we could neither protect effectively nor advance what we saw as the British interest."
Major repeated his commitment to hold a referendum if his government eventually wanted to join a single currency, saying he would then respect the British people's verdict.
However, it appeared that Major would be unable to damp down the internal debate in the Conservative Party.

John Redwood, a former cabinet minister who last year challenged Major for the party leadership, will call on Sunday for Britain to attempt to prevent other EU states joining the single currency unless their economies are strong enough.

In an independent television interview the text of which was made public in advance, Redwood said some EU states seemed to want to join without meeting strict criteria on matters such as public debt laid down in the EU's Maastricht Treaty.

"Other members states want to stretch and weave and duck around the treaty. I think Britain should be the custodian of the treaty. It should say to the other member states "No, this isn't what the treaty had in mind'," Redwood said.
